claims.claim: Six types of dopaminergic neurons (DANs) mediate the hunger and satiety controls.
claims.source: These controls are mediated by six types of dopaminergic neurons (DANs).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experiments blocking and activating specific DANs.

claims.claim: Manipulating DANs can inhibit food-seeking behavior in hungry flies.
claims.source: By manipulating these DANs, we could inhibit food-seeking behavior in hungry flies or promote food seeking in fed flies.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments using UAS-TrpA1 and UAS-shits1 to activate or block DANs.

claims.claim: Manipulating DANs can promote food seeking in fed flies.
claims.source: By manipulating these DANs, we could inhibit food-seeking behavior in hungry flies or promote food seeking in fed flies.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments using UAS-TrpA1 and UAS-shits1 to activate or block DANs.

claims.claim: The DANs potentially receive multiple inputs of hunger and satiety signals.
claims.source: Finally, we show that the DANs potentially receive multiple inputs of hunger and satiety signals.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNAi knockdown experiments of various receptors in DANs.

claims.claim: The MB is an information-rich central circuit in the fly brain that controls hunger-driven food-seeking behavior.
claims.source: This work demonstrates an information-rich central circuit in the fly brain that controls hunger-driven food-seeking behavior.
claims.evidence: This is the overall conclusion of the study based on all the experimental findings.

claims.claim: The main nutrient- and energy-sensing organs in vertebrates are stomach, gut, and white adipose tissue.
claims.source: The main nutrient- and energy-sensing organs in vertebrates are stomach, gut, and white adipose tissue (Kairupan et al., 2016; Porte et al., 2002; Small and Bloom, 2004).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: Hormones such as leptin, ghrelin, neuropeptide Y (NPY), and cholecystokinin serve as hunger and satiety signals in the nervous system.
claims.source: Hormones such as leptin, ghrelin, neuropeptide Y (NPY), and cholecystokinin that are secreted by these organs serve as hunger and satiety signals in the nervous system and control how an animal responds to food cues (Kairupan et al., 2016; Porte et al., 2002; Sternson et al., 2013; Sternson and Eiselt, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: Hormonal signals play important roles in mediating hunger control in Drosophila.
claims.source: Hormonal signals also play important roles in mediating hunger control in the fruit fly Drosophila; these include insulin-like peptides, the two homologs of mammalian NPY (Neuropeptide F, NPF, and short Neuropeptide F, sNPF), the homolog of mammalian leptin (Unpaired 2, Upd2), the insect analog of glucagon (adipokinetic hormone, AKH), and a handful of other neuropeptides and metabolites (Dus et al., 2015; Inagaki et al., 2014; Jourjine et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2004; Pool and Scott, 2014; Rajan and Perrimon, 2012; Root et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2005; Yu et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: Flies primarily rely on olfactory cues to locate food.
claims.source: Flies primarily rely on olfactory cues to locate food.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge about fly behavior.

claims.claim: Starvation sensitizes the olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) for attractive odors via the cooperation of insulin and sNPF signaling pathways.
claims.source: Starvation sensitizes the olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) for attractive odors via the cooperation of insulin and sNPF signaling pathways (Root et al., 2011) and, in parallel, dampens the activity of ORNs for aversive odors through the neuropeptide tachykinin released from interneurons in the antennal lobe (Ko et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: Starvation dampens the activity of ORNs for aversive odors through the neuropeptide tachykinin released from interneurons in the antennal lobe.
claims.source: Starvation sensitizes the olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) for attractive odors via the cooperation of insulin and sNPF signaling pathways (Root et al., 2011) and, in parallel, dampens the activity of ORNs for aversive odors through the neuropeptide tachykinin released from interneurons in the antennal lobe (Ko et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: The neuropeptide CCHamide is involved in hunger-induced modulation in ORNs.
claims.source: Another neuropeptide, CCHamide, is also involved in hunger-induced modulation in ORNs (Farhan et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: A pair of NPF-expressing neurons in the adult brain encode odor attractiveness.
claims.source: A pair of NPF-expressing neurons in the adult brain have been shown to encode odor attractiveness (Beshel and Zhong, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: Starvation heightens the activity of the NPF neurons.
claims.source: Importantly, starvation heightens the activity of the NPF neurons, but how the graded NPF signal is translated into approach behavior is not known.
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: Food odors detected by specific ORNs are relayed by antennal lobe projection neurons to the mushroom body (MB) and lateral horn (LH).
claims.source: Food odors detected by specific ORNs are relayed by antennal lobe projection neurons to the mushroom body (MB) and lateral horn (LH) (Jefferis et al., 2007; Lin et al., 2007; Stocker et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: The LH plays a major role in innate olfactory behavior.
claims.source: It has been suggested that the LH plays a major role in innate olfactory behavior (de Belle and Heisenberg, 1994; Heimbeck et al., 2001; Jefferis et al., 2007; Parnas et al., 2013; Strutz et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: Neural modulation in the LH has been shown to regulate feeding behavior in Drosophila larvae.
claims.source: Neural modulation in the LH has been shown to regulate feeding behavior in Drosophila larvae.
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: Brief presentation of appetizing odors causes voracious feeding on sugar-rich food even in fed larvae; a process involving NPF neurons and dopaminergic neurons projecting to the LH.
claims.source: Brief presentation of appetizing odors causes voracious feeding on sugar-rich food even in fed larvae; a process involving NPF neurons and dopaminergic neurons projecting to the LH (Wang et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: The MB is conventionally considered to be an olfactory learning and memory center.
claims.source: In contrast to the LH, the MB is conventionally considered to be an olfactory learning and memory center (de Belle and Heisenberg, 1994; Heisenberg, 2003; Keene and Waddell, 2007; McGuire et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: The MB is composed of around 2200 intrinsic neurons called Kenyon Cells (KC).
claims.source: The MB is composed of around 2200 intrinsic neurons called Kenyon Cells (KC), which extend parallel axonal fibers to form the γ, α′β′, and αβ lobes of the MB (Aso et al., 2014a; Crittenden et al., 1998; Lin et al., 2007; Strausfeld et al., 2003; Tanaka et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: Each KC receives inputs from a random combination of antennal lobe projection neurons.
claims.source: Each KC receives inputs from a random combination of antennal lobe projection neurons (Caron et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: The KC outputs converge onto 21 types of 34 MB output neurons (MBONs).
claims.source: The KC outputs converge onto 21 types of 34 MB output neurons (MBONs).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: The dendrites of each MBON type arborize in specific compartments of the MB lobes.
claims.source: The dendrites of each MBON type arborize in specific compartments of the MB lobes, and all MBON types together innervate 15 distinct compartments that tile the MB lobes (Aso et al., 2014a).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: About 130 MB-innervating DANs of 20 cell types have been identified.
claims.source: About 130 MB-innervating DANs of 20 cell types have been identified (Aso et al., 2014a).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: Distinct types of DANs react selectively to punishment or reward stimuli to potentiate or depress KC-to-MBON synapses in specific compartments.
claims.source: Distinct types of DANs react selectively to punishment or reward stimuli to potentiate or depress KC-to-MBON synapses in specific compartments; a process believed to be the neural basis of olfactory associative learning (Aso et al., 2012; Aso and Rubin, 2016; Burke et al., 2012; Das et al., 2014; Galili et al., 2014; Hige et al., 2015a; Huetteroth et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2014b; Liu et al., 2012; Owald et al., 2015; Yamagata et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: The MB is required for innate odor attraction but not repulsion.
claims.source: It was initially reported that the MB is required for innate odor attraction but not repulsion (Wang et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: Recent studies suggest that the MB circuit also regulates innate odor repulsion.
claims.source: However, recent studies suggest that the MB circuit also regulates innate odor repulsion (Bräcker et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2015; Owald et al., 2015; Perisse et al., 2016; Siju et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: Blocking the MBONs innervating the tips of the horizontal MB lobes impairs a fly's response to aversive odors.
claims.source: Blocking the MBONs innervating the tips of the horizontal MB lobes impairs a fly's response to aversive odors (Lewis et al., 2015; Owald et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: Starvation controls sugar memory expression by modulating odor-evoked responses in MBONs via other neurons in the MB circuit.
claims.source: It has been proposed that starvation controls sugar memory expression by modulating odor-evoked responses in these MBONs via other neurons in the MB circuit (Perisse et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: MBONs respond to CO2 and mediate CO2-induced avoidance behavior in both fed and starved flies.
claims.source: The same MBONs also respond to CO2 and mediate CO2-induced avoidance behavior in both fed and starved flies (Lewis et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: Blocking neurotransmission of the KCs impairs CO2 avoidance only in hungry flies, but not in fed flies.
claims.source: However, blocking neurotransmission of the KCs impairs CO2 avoidance only in hungry flies, but not in fed flies (Bräcker et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: Average yeast food-seeking performance increases linearly with the duration of food deprivation.
claims.source: At the population level, average yeast food-seeking performance increased linearly with the duration of food deprivation, suggesting that hunger regulates food-seeking behavior in a graded manner within a high dynamic range (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the behavioral assay results shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Hunger regulates food-seeking behavior in a graded manner within a high dynamic range.
claims.source: At the population level, average yeast food-seeking performance increased linearly with the duration of food deprivation, suggesting that hunger regulates food-seeking behavior in a graded manner within a high dynamic range (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the linear relationship between starvation time and food-seeking performance.

claims.claim: Flies starved for 24 hr did not seek a water-only drop.
claims.source: Flies starved for 24 hr did not seek a water-only drop, confirming that they were attracted to yeast in this assay (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the behavioral assay results shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: orco and Ir8a mutant flies could not locate yeast drops.
claims.source: We found that orco and Ir8a mutant flies could not locate yeast drops (Figure 1B), indicating that flies relied on their sense of smell to find the target.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the behavioral assay results shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Flies relied on their sense of smell to find the yeast target.
claims.source: We found that orco and Ir8a mutant flies could not locate yeast drops (Figure 1B), indicating that flies relied on their sense of smell to find the target.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the inability of olfactory receptor mutants to locate yeast.

claims.claim: Flies use both OR and IR systems to smell yeast odor.
claims.source: This result is consistent with previous findings that flies use both OR and IR systems to smell yeast odor (Gorter et al., 2016; Libert et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature and supported by the current experimental results.

claims.claim: All three major types of KCs—γ, α′β′, and αβ neurons—are important for yeast food-seeking behavior.
claims.source: All three major types of KCs—γ, α′β′, and αβ neurons labeled by MB131B-splitGAL4, MB005B-splitGAL4, and MB008B-splitGAL4, respectively—were found to be important for yeast food-seeking behavior (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by blocking these neurons with UAS-shits1 and observing impaired food-seeking behavior.

claims.claim: Flies whose KCs were blocked did not show any sign of locomotion defects.
claims.source: Flies whose KCs were blocked did not show any sign of locomotion defects and they performed normally when assayed at the permissive temperature of 23°C (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral assays at permissive temperature.

claims.claim: Five MBON types—MBON-γ1pedc>αβ, MBON-β2β′2a, MBON-γ2α′1, MBON-α′2, and MBON-α3—are critical for yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies.
claims.source: In summary, we have identified five MBON types—MBON-γ1pedc>αβ, MBON-β2β′2a, MBON-γ2α′1, MBON-α′2, and MBON-α3—that are critical for yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by blocking these MBONs with UAS-shits1 and observing impaired food-seeking behavior.

claims.claim: Not all positive-valence MBONs are required for yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies.
claims.source: Interestingly, not all positive-valence MBONs are required for yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the screening results of different MBON types.

claims.claim: Only MBON-γ1pedc>αβ and MBON-γ2α′1 encode positive valence and drive approach behavior among the five identified MBONs.
claims.source: Of the five MBONs we identified, only MBON-γ1pedc>αβ and MBON-γ2α′1 encode positive valence and drive approach behavior; the other three MBONs elicit neither approach nor avoidance behavior when optogenetically activated (Aso et al., 2014b).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: All five MBONs required for yeast food-seeking are also important for hungry flies to seek and approach sources of ACV and banana odor.
claims.source: We found that all five MBONs required for yeast food-seeking are also important for hungry flies to seek and approach sources of ACV and banana odor (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by blocking these MBONs and testing with different food odors.

claims.claim: The three major KC populations are required for ACV- and banana odor-seeking behavior.
claims.source: We also tested the three major KC populations and found that they were also required for ACV- and banana odor-seeking behavior (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by blocking these KCs and testing with different food odors.

claims.claim: The KCs and the five MBONs pathways are generally involved in regulating food odor-seeking behavior in hungry flies.
claims.source: These results indicate that the KCs and the five MBONs pathways we identified using the yeast food-seeking assay are generally involved in regulating food odor-seeking behavior in hungry flies.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the results with multiple food odors.

claims.claim: All five MBONs showed hunger-dependent changes in their responses to yeast odor.
claims.source: All five MBONs showed hunger-dependent changes in their responses to yeast odor (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo calcium imaging experiments.

claims.claim: Starvation potentiated MBON-γ1pedc>αβ response to yeast odor.
claims.source: Interestingly, starvation modulated the two positive-valence MBONs contrastingly: it potentiated MBON-γ1pedc>αβ and depressed MBON-γ2α′1 (Figure 5A and B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo calcium imaging experiments.

claims.claim: Starvation depressed MBON-γ2α′1 response to yeast odor.
claims.source: Interestingly, starvation modulated the two positive-valence MBONs contrastingly: it potentiated MBON-γ1pedc>αβ and depressed MBON-γ2α′1 (Figure 5A and B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo calcium imaging experiments.

claims.claim: Hunger-dependent potentiation was observed in MBON-α3.
claims.source: Hunger-dependent potentiation was also observed in MBON-α3 (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo calcium imaging experiments.

claims.claim: Starvation depressed the response to yeast odor in MBON-β2β′2a and MBON-α′2.
claims.source: In MBON-β2β′2a and MBON-α′2, starvation depressed the neurons' response to yeast odor (Figure 5D and E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo calcium imaging experiments.

claims.claim: The reduced hunger-dependent odor response for MBON-γ2α′1 and MBON-α′2 was more pronounced for diluted odors.
claims.source: We note that the reduced hunger-dependent odor response for MBON-γ2α′1 and MBON-α′2 was more pronounced for diluted odors (Figure 5B and E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo calcium imaging experiments with diluted odors.

claims.claim: MBON-γ2α′1 and MBON-α′2 are more sensitive to changes in odor concentration when the fly is starved.
claims.source: Therefore, these neurons are more sensitive to changes in odor concentration (at least for the concentration range that we tested) when the fly is starved.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the more pronounced response changes to diluted odors.

claims.claim: The starvation-induced modification likely happens at the KC-to-MBON synapses.
claims.source: Since an overall increase or decrease in the responses of KCs to yeast odor should result in a general increase or decrease in odor-evoked responses in the MBONs, the bi-directional tuning suggests that the starvation-induced modification likely happens at the KC-to-MBON synapses.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the bi-directional modulation of MBON responses and the lack of changes in KC responses.

claims.claim: No difference in food odor-evoked calcium transients was observed in the entire KC population between fed and starved flies.
claims.source: It has been shown that when food odor-evoked calcium transients are measured from the cell bodies of the entire KC population, no difference was observed between fed and starved flies (Beshel and Zhong, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: Yeast odor-evoked responses in MB lobe compartments innervated by the five food-seeking MBONs did not differ between fed and hungry flies.
claims.source: Consistent with previous findings, the yeast odor-evoked responses in these compartments did not differ between fed and hungry flies (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging experiments in KC compartments.

claims.claim: Ca2+ signal in the α′2 compartment decreased in response to yeast odor in both fed and hungry flies.
claims.source: However, unexpectedly, we found that Ca2+ signal in the α′2 compartment decreased in response to yeast odor in both fed and hungry flies (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging experiments in KC compartments.

claims.claim: Starvation-induced tuning in yeast odor-evoked responses in the five MBONs is not due to changes in the responses of KCs to yeast odor.
claims.source: Overall, our findings and those of others (Beshel and Zhong, 2013) suggest that starvation-induced tuning in yeast odor-evoked responses in the five MBONs is not due to changes in the responses of KCs to yeast odor, supporting that the modulations happen at the KC-to-MBON synapses.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of changes in KC responses and the observed changes in MBON responses.

claims.claim: MBON-γ1pedc>αβ is GABAergic.
claims.source: MBON-γ1pedc>αβ is GABAergic and has been shown to promote appetitive memory expression by inhibiting the activity of MBONs innervating the β′2 zones (Aso et al., 2014a; Perisse et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: MBON-γ1pedc>αβ promotes appetitive memory expression by inhibiting the activity of MBONs innervating the β′2 zones.
claims.source: MBON-γ1pedc>αβ is GABAergic and has been shown to promote appetitive memory expression by inhibiting the activity of MBONs innervating the β′2 zones (Aso et al., 2014a; Perisse et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: RNAi knockdown of GABA biosynthesis in MBON-γ1pedc>αβ resulted in yeast food-seeking defect.
claims.source: RNAi knockdown of GABA biosynthesis in MBON-γ1pedc>αβ using MB112C-splitGAL4 and two independent UAS-GAD-RNAi lines (Koganezawa et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2014a) resulted in the same yeast food-seeking defect caused by blocking the neurons' neurotransmission (Figures 6A and 3A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that MBON-γ1pedc>αβ regulates yeast food-seeking behavior through its release of GABA.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: MBON-γ1pedc>αβ regulates yeast food-seeking behavior through its release of GABA.
claims.source: RNAi knockdown of GABA biosynthesis in MBON-γ1pedc>αβ using MB112C-splitGAL4 and two independent UAS-GAD-RNAi lines (Koganezawa et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2014a) resulted in the same yeast food-seeking defect caused by blocking the neurons' neurotransmission (Figures 6A and 3A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that MBON-γ1pedc>αβ regulates yeast food-seeking behavior through its release of GABA.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the RNAi knockdown results.

claims.claim: Knockdown of GABA-A receptors in MBON-γ5β′2a and MBON-β′2mp revealed strong impairment of yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies.
claims.source: Knockdown of GABA-A receptors using two independent UAS-Rdl-RNAi lines, together with VT1211-GAL4 labeling of MBON-γ5β′2a and MBON-β′2mp, revealed strong impairment of yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: Blocking neurotransmission of MBON-γ5β′2a and MBON-β′2mp exhibited a significant increase in yeast food-seeking behavior when flies were food-satiated at a restrictive 32°C.
claims.source: Furthermore, when UAS-shits1 was expressed with VT1211-GAL4, the flies exhibited a significant increase in yeast food-seeking behavior when they were food-satiated at a restrictive 32°C, but not at a permissive 23°C (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by blocking neurotransmission experiments.

claims.claim: The GABAergic pathway is used to control innate hunger-driven food-seeking behavior.
claims.source: These results support the idea that the GABAergic pathway is used to control innate hunger-driven food-seeking behavior.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the results of GABA and GABA receptor manipulations.

claims.claim: Knockdown of GABA-A receptor in MBON-α1 resulted in decreased yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies.
claims.source: Knockdown of the GABA-A receptor with two independent RNAi lines and MB310C-splitGAL4 that specifically labels MBON-α1 resulted in decreased yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: Blocking the neurotransmission of MBON-α1 promoted yeast food-seeking behavior in fed flies at a restrictive 32°C.
claims.source: Consistently, blocking the neurotransmission of MBON-α1 with MB310C-splitGAL4 and UAS-shits1 promoted yeast food-seeking behavior in fed flies at a restrictive 32°C, but not at a permissive 23°C (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by blocking neurotransmission experiments.

claims.claim: When flies are starved, increased GABA release from MBON-γ1pedc>αβ inhibits MBON-γ5β′2a/MBON-β′2mp and MBON-α1 via the GABA-A receptor.
claims.source: These results suggest that when flies are starved, increased GABA release from MBON-γ1pedc>αβ inhibits MBON-γ5β′2a/MBON-β′2mp and MBON-α1 via the GABA-A receptor.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the results of GABA and GABA receptor manipulations.

claims.claim: Suppression of MBON-γ5β′2a/MBON-β′2mp and MBON-α1 positively biases flies' responses toward yeast odor.
claims.source: In turn, suppression of MBON-γ5β′2a/MBON-β′2mp and MBON-α1 positively biases flies' responses toward yeast odor (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the results of GABA and GABA receptor manipulations.

claims.claim: Blockage of PPL1-α3, PAM-β2β′2a, PAM-β′2a, PPL1-α′2α2, and PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs strongly impaired the performances of hungry flies in yeast food-seeking behavior at a restrictive 32°C.
claims.source: Blockage of the neurotransmission of PPL1-α3, PAM-β2β′2a, PAM-β′2a, PPL1-α′2α2, and PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs with UAS-shits1 strongly impaired the performances of hungry flies in yeast food-seeking behavior at a restrictive 32°C, but not at a permissive 23°C (Figure 7A–E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by blocking neurotransmission experiments.

claims.claim: Hunger promotes dopamine release in PPL1-α3, PAM-β2β′2a, PAM-β′2a, PPL1-α′2α2, and PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs.
claims.source: These results suggest that the corresponding DANs for MBON-α3, MBON-β2β′2a, MBON-α′2, and MBON-γ2α′1 play important roles in regulating yeast food-seeking behavior and that hunger promotes dopamine release in these DANs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the blockage experiments.

claims.claim: PPL1-γ1pedc DANs repress the activity of MBON-γ1pedc>αβ, thereby mediating the hunger control of sugar memory expression.
claims.source: The PPL1-γ1pedc DANs have been shown to repress the activity of MBON-γ1pedc>αβ, thereby mediating the hunger control of sugar memory expression (Perisse et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: Artificial activation of the PPL1-γ1pedc DANs reduced yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies at a restrictive 32°C.
claims.source: Consistently, artificial activation of the PPL1-γ1pedc DANs with UAS-TrpA1, a heat-sensitive cation channel transgene (Hamada et al., 2008), reduced yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies at a restrictive 32°C (Figure 7F), but not at a permissive 23°C (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by activation experiments.

claims.claim: The fruit fly uses the same PPL1-γ1pedc-to-MBON-γ1pedc>αβ neural pathway to mediate hunger control for both innate and learned food-related olfactory cues.
claims.source: These results indicate that the fruit fly uses the same PPL1-γ1pedc-to-MBON-γ1pedc>αβ neural pathway to mediate hunger control for both innate and learned food-related olfactory cues and that hunger inhibits rather than promotes the release of dopamine by PPL1-γ1pedc DANs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the activation and blockage experiments.

claims.claim: Hunger inhibits rather than promotes the release of dopamine by PPL1-γ1pedc DANs.
claims.source: These results indicate that the fruit fly uses the same PPL1-γ1pedc-to-MBON-γ1pedc>αβ neural pathway to mediate hunger control for both innate and learned food-related olfactory cues and that hunger inhibits rather than promotes the release of dopamine by PPL1-γ1pedc DANs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the activation and blockage experiments.

claims.claim: Blockage of PPL1-γ1pedc DANs is sufficient to promote sugar memory expression.
claims.source: Blockage of PPL1-γ1pedc DANs is sufficient to promote sugar memory expression (Krashes et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: Blocking the neurotransmission of PPL1-γ1pedc DANs promotes yeast food-seeking behavior in fed flies at a restrictive 32°C.
claims.source: Indeed, blocking the neurotransmission of PPL1-γ1pedc DANs with UAS-shits1 also promotes yeast food-seeking behavior in fed flies at a restrictive 32°C (Figure 7G), but not at a permissive 23°C (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by blocking neurotransmission experiments.

claims.claim: Artificial activation of PPL1-α3, PAM-β2β′2a, PAM-β′2a, PPL1-α′2α2, and PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs made flies approach yeast food even when they were well fed.
claims.source: Strikingly, in all cases, driving the expression of UAS-TrpA1 with split-GAL4 lines that specifically label these DANs made flies approach yeast food even when they were well fed (Figure 7H–L and Figure 7—figure supplement 1H–L).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by activation experiments.

claims.claim: The behavioral phenotypes observed are unlikely due to olfactory learning.
claims.source: However, the behavioral phenotypes we observed here are unlikely due to olfactory learning.
claims.evidence: This is argued based on the mismatch between expected learning effects and observed behaviors, and conditioning experiments.

claims.claim: Pairing odors with artificial activation of PPL1-α3, PPL1-α′2α2, and PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs induces aversive olfactory memories.

results.result: Hunger regulates food-seeking behavior in a graded manner. Average yeast food-seeking performance increases linearly with starvation duration (0-24 hr), and flies starved for 24 hr do not seek water-only drops, confirming attraction to yeast specifically.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 and C128 are supported by behavioral data in Figure 1A showing a linear relationship between starvation time and food-seeking performance, with appropriate controls (water-only). The graded response and specificity for food are well-demonstrated.

results.result: Flies rely on olfaction to locate yeast food, using both OR and IR olfactory systems. Mutants lacking orco or Ir8a co-receptors cannot locate yeast drops.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44 are supported by behavioral data in Figure 1B showing that orco and Ir8a mutants fail to locate yeast, demonstrating olfactory dependence. This is consistent with prior literature (C44) and provides appropriate genetic controls.

results.result: All three major KC types (γ, α'β', and αβ) are required for yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies. Blocking KCs with UAS-shits1 at 32°C impairs food-seeking without causing locomotion defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46 are supported by behavioral data in Figure 2 showing impaired food-seeking when each KC type is blocked at 32°C but not 23°C, with appropriate temperature and locomotion controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

results.result: Five MBON types (MBON-γ1pedc>αβ, MBON-β2β'2a, MBON-γ2α'1, MBON-α'2, and MBON-α3) are critical for yeast food-seeking in hungry flies. Not all positive-valence MBONs are required, and only two of the five encode positive valence.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 are supported by systematic screening of 36 GAL4 lines (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) with appropriate temperature controls. The identification of five specific MBONs with varied valence properties is well-documented.

results.result: The five identified MBONs and three KC populations are generally required for seeking multiple food odors (yeast, ACV, banana), not just yeast odor specifically.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52 are supported by behavioral data in Figure 4 and supplements showing that blocking these neurons impairs seeking of ACV and banana odors, demonstrating generality across food odors with appropriate controls.

results.result: Starvation bi-directionally modulates MBON responses to yeast odor in a cell-type-specific manner. MBON-γ1pedc>αβ and MBON-α3 are potentiated, while MBON-γ2α'1, MBON-β2β'2a, and MBON-α'2 are depressed by hunger.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C59 are supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 5 showing differential modulation of MBON responses between fed and hungry states. The bi-directional modulation is well-documented with appropriate statistical analysis and concentration-dependence studies.

results.result: Starvation-induced modulation occurs at KC-to-MBON synapses rather than in KCs themselves. KC responses to yeast odor do not differ between fed and hungry flies in the relevant compartments.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C64 are supported by calcium imaging of KC compartments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) showing no hunger-dependent changes in KC responses, combined with bi-directional MBON modulation. This inference is logical given the data, though C63 notes an unexpected decrease in α'2 compartment requiring further investigation.

results.result: A GABAergic pathway from MBON-γ1pedc>αβ to MBON-γ5β'2a/MBON-β'2mp and MBON-α1 controls hunger-driven food-seeking. Starvation increases GABA release from MBON-γ1pedc>αβ, inhibiting downstream MBONs via GABA-A receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C75 are supported by RNAi knockdown experiments (Figure 6) showing that GAD knockdown in MBON-γ1pedc>αβ and Rdl knockdown in target MBONs impair food-seeking in hungry flies, while blocking target MBONs promotes seeking in fed flies. The GABAergic mechanism is well-demonstrated with multiple independent RNAi lines and appropriate controls.

results.result: Six types of DANs mediate hunger control of food-seeking. Blocking PPL1-α3, PAM-β2β'2a, PAM-β'2a, PPL1-α'2α2, and PPL1-γ2α'1 impairs food-seeking in hungry flies, while PPL1-γ1pedc shows opposite regulation (hunger inhibits rather than promotes dopamine release).
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C83 are supported by DAN manipulation experiments (Figure 7) showing that blocking five DAN types impairs food-seeking in hungry flies, while activating PPL1-γ1pedc reduces seeking and blocking it promotes seeking in fed flies. Temperature controls and consistency with prior literature (C78, C82) support the findings.

results.result: Artificial activation of five DAN types (PPL1-α3, PAM-β2β'2a, PAM-β'2a, PPL1-α'2α2, PPL1-γ2α'1) promotes food-seeking in fed flies. These effects are unlikely due to olfactory learning based on mismatch with expected learning outcomes and conditioning experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87 are supported by TrpA1 activation experiments (Figure 7H-L) and conditioning controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 2). The argument against learning effects is reasonable given the mismatch between known learning valences and observed behaviors, though the learning control experiments show some limitations.

results.result: The dopamine receptor DAMB mediates hunger control both pre-synaptically (in KCs) and post-synaptically (in MBONs). DAMB mutants and DAMB knockdown in KCs or specific MBONs impair food-seeking behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C96 are supported by mutant analysis (Figure 8A) and cell-type-specific RNAi knockdown (Figure 8B-G) with two independent RNAi lines. The dual pre- and post-synaptic role is well-demonstrated, though the authors acknowledge that direct DAMB localization in MBON dendrites remains to be shown.

results.result: Starvation differentially modulates odor-evoked responses in DANs: decreasing responses in PPL1-γ1pedc and increasing in PPL1-α3, with no changes in PAM-β2β'2a and PPL1-α'2α2. The contrasting modulation of PPL1-γ1pedc and MBON-γ1pedc>αβ suggests modulation occurs at or downstream of KCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99, C101-C102 are supported by calcium imaging of DANs (Figure 9A-D) showing differential hunger modulation. The inference about modulation site (C102) is logical given the contrasting responses in neurons innervating the same compartment.

results.result: Starvation increases DSyd-1-GFP intensity (active zone marker) in PPL1-γ2α'1, PAM-β2β'2a, and PPL1-α'2α2 DANs without changing DenMark intensity, suggesting increased active zone density or size. No changes were detected in PPL1-γ1pedc or PPL1-α3.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C106 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 9—figure supplement 1) with appropriate controls (DenMark). However, the authors acknowledge that further experiments with endogenous active zone proteins are needed to fully support the conclusion about active zone changes. The interpretation is reasonable but requires validation.

results.result: Serotonin regulates hunger-evoked food-seeking through PPL1-γ2α'1 and PPL1-γ1pedc DANs via different receptors (5HT1B and 5HT2A, respectively). Blocking serotoninergic neurons impairs food-seeking in hungry flies, while activation promotes seeking in fed flies.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C115 are supported by manipulation of serotoninergic neurons (Figure 10A-B) and receptor-specific RNAi knockdown (Figure 10C-F) with two independent RNAi lines. The differential receptor usage is well-demonstrated and provides a mechanism for opposing DAN regulation.

results.result: Multiple hunger signals (NPF, sNPF) regulate DANs in a cell-type-specific manner. NPFR and sNPFR knockdown in different DAN types differentially affects food-seeking, with PPL1-γ1pedc requiring both receptors and other DANs showing varied requirements.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C122 are supported by systematic RNAi knockdown of NPFR and sNPFR across six DAN types (Figure 11A-L) with two independent RNAi lines. The cell-type-specific regulation is well-documented, though direct receptor expression and functional connectivity remain to be demonstrated.

results.result: Satiety signals (insulin, AstA) differentially regulate DANs in a cell-type-specific manner. dInR knockdown in PAM-β'2a, PPL1-α'2α2, and PPL1-γ2α'1 promotes food-seeking in fed flies, while DAR1 knockdown affects PPL1-γ2α'1, PPL1-α'2α2, and PAM-β2β'2a.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C125, C131-C134 are supported by RNAi knockdown experiments (Figure 11M-X) with two independent RNAi lines showing differential effects across DAN types. The pattern reveals that some DANs receive only hunger signals, some only satiety signals, and some both, supporting a complex regulatory architecture.

results.result: The MB receives remarkably rich inputs of hunger and satiety signals. RNAi knockdown data suggest potential diverse inputs to MB circuits controlling innate food-seeking behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C126 and C129 are supported by the comprehensive RNAi screening across multiple receptors and DAN types (Figures 10-11, summarized in Figure 12). The diversity of receptor requirements across DANs demonstrates rich regulatory inputs, though direct anatomical and functional connectivity remains to be fully established.

results.result: The mushroom body integrates hunger and satiety signals to control food-seeking behavior through five essential pathways. This demonstrates an information-rich central circuit controlling hunger-driven food-seeking.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C12, C127 represent the main conclusions supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence including behavioral assays, calcium imaging, genetic manipulations, and receptor knockdowns across multiple figures. The integration of hunger/satiety signals through MB circuits is well-demonstrated.

results.result: Hunger tunes MBON responses in a cell-type-specific manner, with the level of odor-evoked response being critical in some MBONs. A putative circuit mechanism is proposed involving differential connectivity to downstream neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C143 are partially supported. C141 is well-supported by calcium imaging data. C142 is a reasonable inference from the unexpected depression of some MBONs required for food-seeking. However, C143 is explicitly labeled as speculation (hypothetical model) and lacks experimental validation. The proposed mechanism requires further testing.

results.result: DAMB functions both pre- and post-synaptically, though prior literature shows DAMB is mainly in axonal processes and absent from dendrites. Current data suggest DAMB might also function in MBON dendrites.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C148 present a tension between prior literature (C147) and current functional data (C146, C148). While the functional requirement for DAMB in MBONs is demonstrated, the authors acknowledge that direct demonstration of DAMB localization in MBON dendrites is still needed. The functional data are strong but anatomical validation is lacking.
